title: Install, test and maintain a basic fluid power system

lessons.title: Fluid power principles and components
lessons.html:
What fluid power is

Fluid power uses a pressurised liquid (hydraulics) or compressed air (pneumatics) to transmit force and motion. On farms and landscape sites you find it in tractor three-point linkages and remotes, front-end loaders, tipping trailers, hydraulic valve actuators, workshop presses, air tools and pneumatic controls in packhouses.

Pascal's principle

Pressure applied to a confined fluid acts equally in all directions. Force = pressure × area. A small force on a small piston produces the same pressure on a large piston, which then exerts a larger force. This is how a hydraulic jack lifts a bakkie.

FeatureHydraulicsPneumatics
MediumOil (incompressible)Air (compressible)
PressureHigh; strong forcesLower; lighter forces
MotionSmooth, precise, holds positionFast, can be springy
LeaksMessy, environmental hazardClean but waste energy

Basic system components

  • Reservoir (hydraulic) or receiver (pneumatic): stores the fluid or air.
  • Pump or compressor: creates flow; pressure develops when flow meets resistance.
  • Filters: keep fluid clean; dirt is the main cause of hydraulic failure. Pneumatic systems also have water separators and lubricators (FRL units).
  • Pressure relief valve: limits maximum pressure to protect the system.
  • Directional control valves: send fluid to one side of an actuator or the other; described by ports and positions, for example a 4/3 valve.
  • Flow control valves: set the speed of actuators.
  • Actuators: cylinders (single or double acting) for straight-line motion; motors for rotation.
  • Hoses, pipes and fittings rated for the system pressure.
  • Gauges to read pressure.

Circuit symbols

Fluid power circuits are drawn with standard ISO 1219 symbols. Learn to read the symbols for pump, relief valve, directional valve, cylinder, filter and tank so you can follow a circuit diagram.

lessons.title: Installing a basic fluid power system safely
lessons.html:
Hazards

Fluid power systems store a lot of energy.

  • Fluid injection: a pinhole leak in a hydraulic hose can inject oil through the skin. It may look minor but is a medical emergency needing urgent surgical attention. Never feel for leaks with your hand; use cardboard.
  • Stored pressure: accumulators and cylinders holding loads keep pressure after the pump stops.
  • Falling loads: loaders, tipping bins and lifted implements can drop if a hose is disconnected or a valve moved. Lower loads to the ground or block them securely.
  • Whipping hoses: a burst hose or loose air line can whip violently.
  • Hot oil and burns, slippery floors, noise from compressors.

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, machinery must be made safe before maintenance: isolate the power source, release stored pressure, and lock out.

Installation steps

  1. Study the circuit diagram and parts list. Check that all components are rated for the maximum system pressure and flow.
  2. Mount the pump, reservoir, valves and actuators securely, aligned to avoid side loads on cylinder rods.
  3. Clean all components and lines before assembly; cap open ports to keep dirt out.
  4. Route hoses with no twisting, sharp bends or rubbing on edges; allow length for movement; use clamps and protective sleeves. Never exceed the hose's minimum bend radius.
  5. Use correct fittings and seals; do not mix thread types. Tighten to the specified torque.
  6. Fill the reservoir with the correct, clean fluid grade through a filter.
  7. For pneumatics, fit an FRL unit (filter, regulator, lubricator) at the supply point and drain valves on receivers.
  8. Label lines and valves as on the diagram.

Personal protection

Wear safety glasses, gloves suited to oils, and safety boots. Clean up spills immediately with absorbent material and dispose of oily waste correctly; never wash oil into drains or soil.

lessons.title: Testing, commissioning and maintaining the system
lessons.html:
Commissioning

  1. Check all connections, levels and that the relief valve is set low initially (or as the procedure specifies).
  2. Make sure people are clear of actuators and the load path.
  3. Start the pump or compressor briefly to check rotation and that it delivers flow.
  4. Bleed air from hydraulic lines and cylinders by cycling actuators slowly through full stroke with no load. Air causes spongy, jerky movement.
  5. Raise the relief valve to the specified setting while watching the gauge. Never set it above the lowest-rated component.
  6. Test each function: correct direction, speed (adjust flow controls), holding under load, and smooth operation.
  7. Check for leaks, temperature rise and noise. Top up fluid after bleeding.

Routine maintenance

TaskWhy
Check fluid level and conditionMilky oil means water; dark or burnt smell means overheating
Replace filters as scheduled or when indicators showDirt causes valve sticking and pump wear
Inspect hoses for cracks, bulges, abrasion and leaking fittingsPrevent bursts and injection injuries
Check cylinder rods for scoring and seals for leaksDamaged rods destroy seals
Drain water from air receivers and filters dailyWater corrodes and damages pneumatic parts
Check pressure settingsConfirm relief valve and regulators are correct

Fault finding

  • Slow actuator: low flow, worn pump, internal leakage, flow control set too low, clogged filter.
  • No movement: no pressure, relief valve stuck open, valve not shifting, load too high.
  • Overheating: relief valve constantly blowing off, low fluid level, blocked cooler.
  • Noisy pump: cavitation from blocked suction strainer, low fluid, air leak in suction.
  • Load creeps down: worn cylinder seals or leaking valve.

Records

Keep a record of settings, fluid type, filter changes, hose replacements with dates, and faults, so recurring problems are spotted.

Key points

  • Force = pressure × area; hydraulics use oil, pneumatics use air.
  • Never check for hydraulic leaks by hand; injection injuries are emergencies.
  • Lower loads, release pressure and lock out before work.
  • Keep fluid clean, bleed air and set relief valves correctly.
  • Inspect hoses, filters and seals regularly and record the work.
